# Genesis 10 – Research Notes (verse by verse)

I didn't find anything on bibleodyssey.org or in the netbible.org notes. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those categories are left out below.

On where Protestant traditions differ: none of the sources I read describe a split along denominational lines in this chapter. Commentators do disagree, mainly on vv. 9, 11 and 25, but they disagree within traditions as much as between them. Where it may help, I've named the commentator so you can place him yourself. Those labels are my own; the pages don't state them.

---

**v. 1**
- One commentary says "generations" is better translated "histories." It is used here for the fourth time, and probably closes the section about these men rather than introducing what follows. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary
- Guzik says the verse shows that people did multiply after the flood, as God had told them to, and that life went on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Constable says the table shows that Yahweh created all peoples (he links Deut 32:8, Amos 9:7 and Acts 17:26). It is a "horizontal" genealogy: it shows political, geographical and ethnic links between tribes rather than tracing a line of ancestors. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-10.html
- Everett says only one of the three sons, Shem, would carry the line of righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/genesis-10.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Japheth fathered the Indo-European peoples, from India to Western Europe. He links Gomer to the Germanic peoples, Magog, Tubal and Meshech to the Russians, Madai to the Medes, and Javan to the Greeks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Ellicott says Magog means the Scythians of the Caucasus, Tubal the Tibareni near the Black Sea, and Meshech the Moschi of Colchis and Armenia. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html
- Henry Morris says Japheth's sons can be recognised as the ancestors of the Indo-European peoples, once you allow for names changing over time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63929/

**v. 3**
- Guzik links Ashkenaz to peoples who settled north of Judea, and Togarmah to the Armenians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/

**v. 4**
- Guzik says linguists see links between Kittim and Cyprus, and between Rodanim and Rhodes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Ellicott says the Kittim were a seafaring people who settled Cyprus, whose chief city was Kitium. He adds that 1 Maccabees calls Alexander king of the Kittim. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik says the dividing of mankind here grew into divisions of language, family and nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- The Hebrew word for "separated" (*parad*) means to divide, disperse or scatter. It is used again of the nations in v. 32. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary
- Clarke thinks v. 5 is said "by way of anticipation," that is, it looks ahead to the later division. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-25.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik identifies Mizraim as Egypt, Put as Libya, and Canaan as the peoples of the land later called Israel. He says Cush split early, with one branch founding Babylon and another Ethiopia. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Ellicott says this Cush is an Asian Ethiopia on the Tigris and Euphrates. From there, he says, the Cushites spread into southern Arabia and later crossed into Nubia and Abyssinia. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**v. 7**
- One source says Cush's sons were apparently peoples of the Arabian coast, where Egypt's influence was strongest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63929/
- Everett notes there are two men named Sheba in this list. The first is Raamah's son here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/genesis-10.html

**v. 8** (the main disagreement in the chapter)
- **Negative reading (the majority):** Guzik says Nimrod was mighty "but not in a good way," and that his name means "let us rebel." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Matthew Henry says Nimrod set out to lord it over his neighbours, and that the spirit of the pre-flood giants of Gen 6:4 came alive again in him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-9.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible glosses "mighty one" as a cruel oppressor and tyrant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-8.htm
- **Gill (a Baptist):** says the phrase is about his role as a ruler, not his size or moral character. He was the first to bring peoples and cities under one government, whether by force or by consent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-8.htm
- **Ellicott (Anglican) disagrees:** "Cush begat" means only that Cush was an ancestor. He calls the "rebel" meaning of the name unscholarly. He says the Bible actually speaks rather well of Nimrod, and that the stories blackening his name only go back to Josephus. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**v. 9**
- **"In defiance of":** Guzik says the phrase was no compliment: Nimrod was an offence in God's sight, a hunter of men. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Keil & Delitzsch say Nimrod hunted in opposition to Jehovah. The proverb, they say, remembered his hunting of men to build an empire by tyranny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-9.htm
- Benson says Nimrod first won favour by ridding the land of wild beasts. He then used hunting as cover to gather men, and became a violent invader of his neighbours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-9.htm
- Clarke notes that the Hebrew word for "hunter" is used elsewhere of hunting men through oppression. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-8.html
- **Positive or neutral:** Ellicott calls "before the LORD" simply "a strong superlative." He pictures Nimrod as a public benefactor who brought order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-9.htm
- The BibleHub study note says the verse both recognises God-given ability and warns that every achievement is open to God's judgement. https://biblehub.com/genesis/10-9.htm
- Translations split the same way: GOD'S WORD has "whom the LORD blessed," while the ISV has "in defiance of the LORD." https://biblehub.com/genesis/10-9.htm
- **Catholic/early church:** Augustine follows the Greek Old Testament: a "giant hunter *against* the Lord." He says a hunter here means a deceiver, oppressor and destroyer. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120116.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia allows either a literal hunter of wild beasts or a "warrior/hero" (*gibbor*). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10741a.htm
- **Debated popular teaching:** Chuck Smith says Nimrod founded the "mystery Babylon" religious system. He also says Nimrod's mother Semiramis was later worshipped as queen of heaven and claimed a virgin birth for him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-8.html
- Gill passes on traditions that identify Nimrod with Bacchus and with the constellation Orion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-9.htm
- Ellicott calls the Orion link "entirely fanciful." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott says Shinar is Babylonia, the lower part of Mesopotamia. Micah 5:6 calls it "the land of Nimrod." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html
- Augustine concludes that Nimrod founded Babylon, the capital over the other cities. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120116.htm
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Gilgamesh also reigns over Erech, though the texts don't name the other cities. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10741a.htm

**v. 11** (a translation question: did Nimrod go to Assyria, or did Asshur leave?)
- **"He (Nimrod) went into Assyria":** Ellicott notes that the Greek, Syriac and Latin versions read "Asshur went forth." But he sides with the Targum and most modern scholars in reading "he went forth into Assyria." https://biblehub.com/genesis/10-11.htm
- Clarke reads it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-11.html
- Barnes gives reasons: the passage is about Nimrod, and Asshur has so far appeared only as the name of a country. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gen/genesis/10-11.html
- **"Asshur went forth":** Gill and Calvin take this to be Shem's son Asshur. In Gill's account, Asshur could not bear Nimrod's tyranny and left. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-11.html
- Benson says the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-11.htm
- Augustine's text reads "Assur." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120116.htm

**v. 12**
- Barnes says "the great city" most naturally refers to Resen, though it could mean Nineveh. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/gen/genesis/10-11.html
- Keil & Delitzsch think the four places formed one large combined capital. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ylt/genesis/10-11.html
- Ellicott says Calah's ruins are still called Nimroud. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**vv. 13–14**
- Ellicott identifies the Pathrusim with Upper Egypt ("land of the south"), and the Casluhim probably with Cassiotis, east of Pelusium. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html

**vv. 15–18**
- Ellicott says Sidon is the only town named among Mizraim's and Canaan's descendants. The rest seem to be wandering tribes, which suggests how old the record is. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html
- Everett says six of the seven nations in Deut 7:1 appear here; only the Perizzites are missing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/genesis-10.html
- One source says these are the tribes Joshua fought. They were conquered slowly, fulfilling Noah's words. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63929/
- Guzik reports a view that Asian peoples descend from the Sinites, presented as what "many people believe." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/

**v. 19**
- One source says Canaan's descendants include the people of Sodom and Gomorrah. It says Noah's curse came true when Israel, descended from Shem, conquered the Canaanites. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary

**v. 21**
- Ellicott says calling Shem "father of all the children of Eber" signals that Peleg's descendants are left out here and saved for Shem's own genealogy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-10.html
- On translation: the BSB reads "the older brother of Japheth," while the NKJV text Guzik uses reads "the brother of Japheth the elder." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/

**v. 22**
- Guzik links Elam to the Persians, Asshur to the Assyrians, Lud to the Lydians and Aram to the Syrians. Arphaxad is the ancestor of Abram. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/

**v. 23**
- Guzik says a region was later named after Uz, and that Job came from there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/

**v. 24**
- The title "Hebrew" comes from Eber's name. It is first used of Abraham in Gen 14:13. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary

**v. 25** (Peleg: what was divided?)
- **Babel (the majority):** Keil & Delitzsch say the earth's population was divided because of the tower of Babel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm
- MacArthur and Henry Morris agree, and MacArthur explicitly rejects continental drift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary
- Barnes points to Ps 55:9, "divide their tongues," as support. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm
- **Physical division of the land:** Clarke favours a physical splitting of the continents. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-25.html
- Chuck Smith mentions continental drift but thinks Babel is more likely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/10-25.html
- **Other suggestions:** Matthew Henry says either Noah shared out the land in an orderly way, or God divided people by confusing their languages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm
- The Cambridge Bible notes Sayce's guess that it refers to canals in Babylonia, or to the split between northern and southern Semites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm
- **Timing:** Gill and Leupold put the division about 100 years after the flood. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/leupold/genesis.xiii.html
- Gill also notes the Jewish view that the name was given in prophecy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm

**vv. 26–29**
- Guzik says Joktan's sons are linked with Arab peoples, and that Jobab may be Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- Keil & Delitzsch say the Arabs call Joktan "Kachtan," the father of the earliest Arabian tribes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/10-25.htm

**vv. 31–32**
- Morris counts 70 nations: 14 from Japheth, 30 from Ham and 26 from Shem. He says all descend from Adam, with no hint of "pre-Adamites." https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary
- Constable notes a suggested link between the 70 nations and the seventy disciples Jesus sent out. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-10.html
- G. Campbell Morgan says this chapter describes the division before the next chapter gives its cause. Babel, he says, was an attempt to escape God's wider purpose. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-10-commentary
- Luther (quoted by Guzik) says the chapter is a mirror. Sin has so marred us that we would not know our own origin unless God's Word told us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-10/
- **Early church:** Augustine counts 72 nations, treating Nimrod as founding a nation of his own. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120116.htm
